summary:
Gyeonggi Province stands under the national framework of South Korea. Gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive and targeted. In 2017 the military ran what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, criminally charging 32 personnel, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

The sharpest documented harm to a transgender person concerns Staff Sergeant Byun Hui-su, compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical or mental handicap. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Daejeon District Court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021, and in March 2024 the Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty.

Legal gender recognition is available and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent that uniformly denied recognition to trans parents of minors; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A landmark 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, though LGBTI organisations can register; an NGO won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 and the government appealed onward, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform for safer school environments.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot flagged from within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

Gyeonggi Province carries its own protective layer on top of that national framework. It enacted South Korea's first student human rights ordinance in 2010, and that ordinance includes non-discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, the provisions most disputed in the 2024-26 repeal wave. Gyeonggi and Seoul are the only two jurisdictions whose ordinances include the right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy.

The ordinance layer is under active political pressure but has not collapsed in Gyeonggi. On 28 April 2024 the Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after adoption, a move pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause. Six regional education offices, Gyeonggi among them, still enforced comparable ordinances at that publication, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition. The opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions, and the Seoul superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024-26 repeal wave targets the sexual-orientation and gender-identity clauses specifically: the campaign that preceded Seoul's abolition was mounted by religious groups and parents objecting to that clause, and the same clauses sit in Gyeonggi's ordinance. Whether Gyeonggi's ordinance survives the wave is not resolved in the sources available here.

Discrimination burden is documented at high rates across South Korean life. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates; 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma; a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
localsOnly:
Gyeonggi's student human rights ordinance is administered by the Superintendent of Public Instruction, who conducts an annual survey on student human rights, and the province marks a Student Human Rights Day. Students in Gyeonggi therefore have an enforceable non-discrimination right grounded in sexual orientation and gender identity that students in provinces without such an ordinance do not.

The ordinance model originated in Gyeonggi: it was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for the province, and other regional education offices later adopted comparable instruments. As of April 2024, Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju still enforced comparable ordinances after Seoul's abolition.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Gyeonggi's ordinance has been amended, challenged or repealed after the April 2024 reporting date is unresolved in the sources available here; the inventory records only that it was in force at that publication.

No Gyeonggi-specific data on enforcement of Military Criminal Act article 92-6, on trans-specific violence within the province, or on local police handling of Pride events is sourced. The Incheon and Busan incidents are the documented event-level cases and are reported at national level.

The National Assembly's stated intention to legislate a national student-rights act is a reported commitment, not a enacted statute; no source here confirms passage.
